setup: This is the strangest civilization in the whole series, and the strangeness is the point. The greatest city in the ancient Americas, home to as many as 200,000 people, left no king lists, no royal portraits, no readable writing, and not one ruler's name. We do not even know what its builders called it. "Teotihuacan" is a Nahuatl name the Aztecs slapped on the ruins seven centuries after the city had already burned. So this opening chapter is about beginnings, but it is also a warning label: nearly everything we say here is inference from stone, pottery, obsidian, and paint, because the highland climate rotted everything else away. The action starts around 100 BCE in the Basin of Mexico, where the obvious candidate for greatness is a city called Cuicuilco. Then a volcano named Xitle buries Cuicuilco under thirty feet of lava and sends thousands of refugees northeast into a side valley with springs, good soil, and the richest obsidian deposits in central Mexico. What they build there should have been a refugee camp. Instead it becomes a planned city laid out on a precise grid, and the question is who could possibly have organized that.

bridge: Chapter 1 left us with a puzzle: around 100 BCE, refugees from a volcano-buried city poured into the Teotihuacan Valley, and within a generation or two somebody had organized 20,000 to 40,000 of them into not a camp but a city, laid out on a precise grid tilted 15.5 degrees east of north. We don't know who that somebody was — no ruler's name survives from any era of this place. What we do know is that whoever it was committed to a master plan that every later builder obeyed for six centuries. Now we watch that plan become monumental.
setup: Within roughly a hundred years of the first grid lines, Teotihuacan builds the skyline it will keep for the next four hundred: the Pyramid of the Sun, the early Pyramid of the Moon, and the broad ceremonial avenue the Aztecs later misnamed the Street of the Dead. The Sun pyramid alone has a footprint nearly the size of the Great Pyramid of Giza, and it goes up in essentially one construction campaign — no draft animals, no metal tools, no wheels, just human labor and staggering organization. The avenue is engineered as theater: it climbs toward the sacred mountain so the Moon pyramid seems to grow out of the hillside, designed by people who understood exactly how to make a person feel small. Even the river is bent to obey the grid. This is the chapter where you grasp the sheer scale of the achievement — and where the comparison to Rome, the city's almost-exact contemporary on the far side of an ocean neither knew existed, starts doing real work.

bridge: By now the city's spine is in place: the Pyramid of the Sun, the great avenue, the river bent to the grid. Chapter 2 showed the scale; this chapter goes looking for the politics, which is hard, because Teotihuacan left no royal records of any kind. What it did leave is buildings that were enlarged, dedicated, and sometimes deliberately buried — and the offerings sealed inside them turn out to be the closest thing this anonymous city has to a chronicle of who held power and when.
setup: Two structures anchor this chapter, one at each end of the Street of the Dead. At the north, the Pyramid of the Moon was rebuilt seven times over 250 years, and each new shell was consecrated with sacrificial burials that grew steadily more lavish — bound captives, imported jaguars and pumas, hundreds of pieces of jade and obsidian — a rising record of a state flexing its reach. At the south, inside the walled Ciudadela, the Temple of the Feathered Serpent went up around 200 CE with over 200 sacrificed warriors buried beneath it, nearly tripling the largest known mass burial in the ancient Old World. And then, around 250 CE, somebody built a blank platform — the Adosada — directly over the temple's carved face, hiding it. A government burying its own showpiece reads as a regime change, a revolution. What kind of order replaced the old one is the deepest question here, because whatever came next chose to express itself through blankness — and stopped depicting individual people at all.

bridge: Three chapters in, we've watched the city rise, build its monuments, and pass through a revolution around 250 CE that left it stranger than ever — anonymous by design, expressing power through blankness rather than royal portraits. But monuments and sacrifice don't explain how a quarter-million people fed, housed, and paid for themselves. This chapter follows the money, and the money is volcanic glass.
setup: By 300 CE Teotihuacan is the economic engine of Mesoamerica, and obsidian is the fuel. In a world with no usable metal, obsidian is the sharpest cutting material going, and the city sits on top of the two best sources in central Mexico — prized green obsidian and everyday gray. It doesn't just use them; it monopolizes the whole chain, with over 400 workshops turning out blades for export across the region. Around that industry the city builds something found nowhere else in the ancient Americas: more than 2,000 walled apartment compounds, each housing 60 to 100 people, with drainage, courtyards, and painted walls, and — unusually — broadly the same plan for rich and poor alike. Whole neighborhoods specialize by craft. Exotic goods flow in from astonishing distances, including mica from possibly 1,800 miles away, buried invisibly beneath temple floors for reasons nobody can explain. What's at stake here is the answer to a basic question: how do you run a city this size with no writing, no coins, no wheels, and no pack animals?

bridge: We've built the monuments and followed the obsidian economy that paid for them; now we meet the people, and they turn out not to be one people at all. The trade networks of Chapter 4 didn't just move goods into Teotihuacan — they moved migrants, and the city that erased its own rulers' names made room for entire foreign communities to keep theirs.
setup: Teotihuacan was a genuinely multiethnic city, something archaeology has confirmed through pottery, architecture, and the chemistry of people's bones. Two enclaves stand out. In the west, the Oaxacan Barrio housed Zapotec migrants from Monte Alban, 250 miles away, who for centuries made their own grayware, buried their dead in Zapotec tombs, and spoke a language as far from their neighbors' as English is from Mandarin. On the east, the Merchants' Barrio housed Gulf Coast people who built round houses in a city of rectangles. These weren't transient traders — they raised children and buried grandparents while staying culturally distinct across generations. The chapter asks why the most powerful city in the hemisphere opened its doors to foreigners, weighing the likeliest answer (it needed their trade goods and their networks) against darker possibilities (forced relocation) and a political one (a city of many peoples is a city no single people can dominate). Around it all, ordinary life: maize, figurines, the dead buried under the kitchen floor — and a peak population so large no American city would match it for a thousand years.

bridge: We've established what Teotihuacan was at home: a planned megacity, an obsidian superpower, a multiethnic capital that hid its rulers' names. What we haven't seen is how far its arm could reach. The trade ties of the last chapters ran deep into the Maya world to the southeast — and in this chapter that reach stops being commercial and turns, on a single recorded day, into something much sharper.
setup: On January 16, 378 CE — a date we can pin exactly, thanks to the Maya Long Count calendar — a warrior named Siyaj K'ahk' arrives at the great Maya city of Tikal, 630 miles away in the Guatemalan jungle. The same day, Tikal's king dies. Within a year a new dynasty sits on the throne, dressed in Teotihuacan war regalia and invoking Teotihuacan gods. This event, the Entrada, is the clearest proof that the anonymous city was a military and political force, not just an economic one. The strangeness is total: everything we know about it comes from Maya inscriptions, while Teotihuacan's own record says nothing — the conqueror is invisible and the conquered brag about being conquered, because the new dynasty turned the foreign connection into a source of legitimacy. Behind it stands a shadowy overlord the Maya called Spearthrower Owl, possibly the only Teotihuacan ruler whose name survives at all — though even that is uncertain. The chapter wrestles with what kind of power could install a dynasty a thousand kilometers away and leave no trace of having done it.

bridge: Across six chapters we've reconstructed almost everything about this city except the one thing every other civilization hands us freely: its inner life, its names, its words. Teotihuacan wrote nothing we can read. So this chapter turns to the only archive it left — the paint on its walls — to ask what these people actually believed, and why a city this powerful chose images over text.
setup: Teotihuacan's religion survives almost entirely as murals and sculpture, uncaptioned, so every deity name we use is borrowed from the Aztecs a thousand years later or invented by modern scholars. Out of the painted walls a pantheon emerges. The Great Goddess presides over a watery paradise at Tepantitla, water streaming from her hands — and in a city that refused to depict individual rulers, she may be the closest thing it had to a public face of power. The goggle-eyed Storm God appears everywhere and survives, almost unchanged, as the Aztec rain god Tlaloc a millennium later. Warrior murals reveal eagle and coyote military orders that prefigure the famous Aztec warrior societies, wielding the atlatl spear-thrower that was the city's signature weapon. And the eerie, faceless stone masks embody the whole principle of the place: the individual erased, the collective everything. Running underneath is the genuine puzzle — did Teotihuacan choose not to write, or did its books simply rot? The answer changes whether its anonymity was a strategy or an accident.

bridge: Seven chapters have built the most powerful city in the ancient Americas: planned grid, Giza-scale pyramids, an obsidian empire of trade, foreign quarters, a dynasty installed in the Maya world, and a pantheon painted on every wall — all of it run by people who left no names. This final chapter is about the two things archaeology still can't explain: how the city died, and why it stayed silent to the end.
setup: Around 550 CE somebody set fire to Teotihuacan — not a wildfire, not an invading army's sack, but a careful, targeted burning of the temples and palaces along the Street of the Dead, while the ordinary apartment compounds were left standing. The pattern points at the state, not the city: an internal revolt against the rulers. What triggered it is the chapter's open question, and the suspects pile up — deforestation from centuries of plaster-making, a rigid post-revolution government, 6th-century drought, raw inequality, a trade network slipping out of the city's grip. The population crashes from 100,000-plus to a fraction within a generation, and the power vacuum reshapes Mesoamerica as rivals like Xochicalco and Cholula rush in. Then the story leaps forward: the Aztecs arrive seven centuries later, name the dead pyramids, and write Teotihuacan into their own creation myth as the birthplace of the sun. The chapter closes on the defining fact of the whole narrative — we can date its founding, its revolution, its conquests, and its fall, yet cannot name a single person who lived there.
